before.title: Plan, Monitor, and Communicate
before.summary: The assessment matters only when it changes care. A complete plan states the problem, intervention, surveillance, and decision points.
before.application: Write a plan that another clinician can execute. Include who will act, what will be measured, when it will be measured, and what finding will trigger escalation.

lesson.heading: Connect cause to intervention
lesson.body: Address reversible barriers such as nausea, constipation, dysphagia, pain, food access, medication timing, and overly restrictive diets. Coordinate with dietitians, nurses, prescribers, speech language pathology, social work, and the patient according to the problem identified.

lesson.heading: Monitor both benefit and harm
lesson.body: Follow intake, weight trajectory, volume status, symptoms, physical findings, function, and relevant laboratory data. A high risk patient who begins aggressive nutrition support may also require focused surveillance for electrolyte shifts, glycemic complications, fluid intolerance, and refeeding risk.

keyPoints: A monitoring plan needs a measure, interval, goal, and action threshold.
Reconcile medicines that may worsen intake or gastrointestinal tolerance.
Escalate urgently when severe intake restriction, unsafe swallowing, major electrolyte risk, or rapid decline is present.

check.question: Which follow up plan is most actionable?
choices: Record meal intake each shift, measure weight under consistent conditions twice weekly, and reassess barriers in 72 hours
Monitor nutrition
Repeat every laboratory test daily forever
Wait until discharge to reassess
check.rationale: An actionable plan identifies what will be measured, how often it will be measured, and when the team will reassess the cause and response.

after.title: Plan, Monitor, and Communicate
after.summary: An assessment becomes a care plan when the team names the problem, acts on its cause, measures benefit and harm, and assigns the next decision.
after.application: State the evidence and uncertainty, the proposed action and responsible clinician, the measure and goal, the review interval, and the finding that triggers escalation. Confirm that the receiving team can carry out the plan.

lesson.heading: Connect cause to intervention
lesson.body: Investigate barriers such as nausea, constipation, dysphagia, pain, food access, and medicine effects before choosing an intervention. A symptom that follows a new medicine suggests a possible contribution, not proof of causation. Review its indication and alternatives with the prescriber, address other plausible causes, and measure the response. Coordinate dietitian, nursing, pharmacy, swallowing, and social support according to the problem; involve the patient in the plan.

lesson.heading: Monitor benefit and harm from the start
lesson.body: Track actual intake and delivered feed, symptoms, weight with fluid balance, clinical condition, and relevant laboratory trends. The supplied book highlights glucose intolerance, electrolyte shifts, and fluid accumulation during parenteral nutrition. High refeeding risk calls for cautious, individualized initiation by an experienced team and planned surveillance, not aggressive feeding followed by optional monitoring. A new electrolyte decline or clinical deterioration requires prompt reassessment of feeding, replacement, and fluid management under the agreed protocol.

lesson.heading: Choose intervals for the patient and setting
lesson.body: NICE CG32 provides adult nutrition-support monitoring examples. In hospital, initially assess intake daily and chart fluid balance during enteral or parenteral support. Check weight daily when fluid balance is a concern; otherwise use weekly weights, reducing frequency with stability. Its laboratory table calls for baseline tests, daily sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine until stable, glucose once or twice daily until stable, and daily magnesium and phosphate when refeeding risk is present. This table chiefly addresses parenteral nutrition and is selectively applicable to oral or enteral support. Acute instability may require more frequent assessment; these are not universal intervals for every patient.

lesson.heading: Separate the patient result from delivery of care
lesson.body: Improved intake or relief of nausea is a patient outcome. Recording intake and completing an agreed medicine review are care processes. In the Proctor implementation framework, fidelity asks whether a pathway was delivered as intended; adherence to its required steps can be one fidelity measure. Adoption concerns initial uptake, acceptability asks whether the pathway is agreeable, and feasibility asks whether it can be carried out in the setting. A completed checklist does not itself prove clinical benefit. Document both the action taken and the patient response, with a named owner, next review, and agreed escalation threshold.

keyPoints: Link the intervention to a supported cause and document uncertainty.
Specify the measure, goal, interval, action threshold, and responsible clinician.
Plan refeeding surveillance before support begins and adapt it to clinical changes.
Measure patient benefit separately from completion of the care process.

check.question: An adult inpatient has nausea and reduced intake. The team has agreed an intake goal and a safe medicine adjustment. Which follow-up plan is most actionable?
choices: Name the nurse to record daily intake against the goal and the prescriber to review response tomorrow, with earlier contact for worsening symptoms or intake below the agreed threshold
Name the nurse to record daily intake but leave the target and response to a low result unspecified
Set an intake goal and a review tomorrow but leave who will assess and act unspecified
Assign a prescriber to review the medicine at discharge without tracking the intake response
check.rationale: The complete plan connects an agreed intervention with ownership, a measure and goal, a review time, and an earlier action trigger. The other plans each leave an essential part of that loop unspecified. The review time is part of this case plan, not a universal nutrition-monitoring interval.

wholeQuestion.question: Which implementation outcome most directly measures whether clinicians deliver an assessment pathway according to its required steps?
choices: Fidelity
Adoption
Acceptability
Feasibility
wholeQuestion.rationale: Fidelity concerns delivery as intended. Adoption concerns initial uptake, acceptability concerns whether the pathway is agreeable, and feasibility concerns whether it can be carried out in the setting. Step adherence is a fidelity measure, not proof of patient benefit.

wholeQuestion.question: A pharmacist review identifies a plausible medicine-related intake barrier. Which evaluation best connects the review to a change in patient care?
choices: Document the agreed medicine action and reassess nausea and intake against the goal
Count completed reviews without recording subsequent actions or patient response
Compare the number of laboratory results before and after the review
Report the admission nutrition-risk score without reassessing the barrier
wholeQuestion.rationale: Link the recommendation to the action taken and the patient response. Review counts are process measures, available laboratory results alone do not show benefit, and an admission screen does not evaluate the effect of the medicine intervention.

wholeQuestion.question: Why should nutrition-monitoring intervals change with clinical risk, care setting, and stability?
choices: A useful interval detects meaningful benefit or harm in time to inform the next decision
The discharge review interval is sufficient for every inpatient because support is prescribed
A single fixed interval permits comparison even when the patient becomes unstable
Normal baseline tests justify keeping the longest interval throughout initiation
wholeQuestion.rationale: NICE CG32 adapts review to the patient and setting and allows intervals to lengthen with stability. Early support or clinical deterioration can require closer observation; normal baseline values do not exclude subsequent shifts.

wholeQuestion.question: Which pair correctly separates a patient outcome from a nutrition-care process measure?
choices: Outcome: intake improves toward the goal; process: scheduled intake records are completed
Outcome: a medicine review is documented; process: nausea resolves
Outcome: the feed order is signed; process: the patient tolerates feeding
Outcome: the assessment checklist is completed; process: intake meets the agreed goal
wholeQuestion.rationale: The patient outcome describes a change in the patient, whereas the process describes delivery or documentation of care. The other pairs reverse those roles. A process can be completed without achieving the intended outcome.

wholeQuestion.question: What makes a nutrition assessment and resulting plan scientifically defensible?
choices: Show the source findings, chosen criteria, confounders and uncertainty, then link the proposed action to a measurable follow-up plan
Use a screening score to establish the diagnosis without assessing its underlying findings
List measurements without stating how they support the problem or intervention
Document the intervention as effective before measuring the patient response
wholeQuestion.rationale: Transparent reasoning makes the evidence, inference, uncertainty, and response assessable. Screening is a risk signal, an unconnected data list does not explain a care decision, and an intended effect should not be recorded as an observed benefit.

wholeQuestion.question: Reduced intake and nausea begin after a new medicine. Which medication-focused intervention best addresses this possible barrier?
choices: Review timing and competing causes, agree a safe adjustment with the prescriber if appropriate, and reassess nausea and intake
Declare the medicine causal from timing alone and stop it without reviewing its indication
Continue the nutrition plan without assessing whether the suspected medicine can be changed safely
Change the medicine with the prescriber but omit any assessment of symptoms or intake afterward
wholeQuestion.rationale: The temporal relationship supports investigation, not certainty. Review the indication and competing causes, agree an appropriate action, and measure the response. The other choices prematurely infer causality, leave the barrier unassessed, or fail to evaluate the intervention.

fourIndividualChoicesReviewed.review: Temporal association alone is insufficient to assign causation or stop therapy indiscriminately.

wholeQuestion.question: An adult at high refeeding risk is beginning cautiously prescribed nutrition support. Which monitoring plan best covers benefit and safety?
choices: Arrange baseline and risk-appropriate repeat electrolytes and glucose, follow intake and fluid and clinical status, and assign review times, action thresholds, and an owner
Follow daily intake and weight with an owner, but defer electrolyte checks until symptoms develop
Arrange repeat electrolytes and glucose but omit fluid balance, intake, and clinical reassessment
Copy a stable outpatient schedule without adapting its intervals to initiation and high refeeding risk
wholeQuestion.rationale: Prospective surveillance must cover biochemical shifts and the patient response, including fluid balance and actual intake. Symptom-triggered tests alone may miss early changes; laboratory tests alone omit bedside information; a stable outpatient schedule does not establish an appropriate high-risk initiation plan. Use the applicable specialist protocol to set frequencies and actions.

wholeQuestion.question: What information most clearly closes the loop after a nutrition recommendation?
choices: The agreed action, responsible clinician, measure and goal, review time, and escalation trigger
The action and measurement goal, with responsibility left to whichever team reads the note
The responsible clinician and a general monitoring instruction, without a measure or review time
The measurements and review date, with no decision planned if the goal is missed
wholeQuestion.rationale: The first plan assigns responsibility and connects an action to measurable follow-up and a response to concerning findings. Each alternative omits ownership, operational measurement and timing, or the decision needed after reassessment.

wholeQuestion.question: Under the NICE CG32 adult nutrition-support monitoring examples, which weight schedule best fits a stable patient without fluid concerns and a patient with new edema during parenteral nutrition?
choices: Weekly weight for the stable patient and daily weight when fluid balance is a concern
Daily weight for the stable patient and weekly weight during new edema
Monthly weight for both patients from the first day of support
Weekly weight for both patients regardless of changing fluid balance
wholeQuestion.rationale: NICE Table 1 uses daily weight when fluid balance is a concern, otherwise weekly with reduced frequency as stability permits. Interpret the weight trend with fluid balance; new edema can reflect fluid gain rather than improved nutrition.

fourIndividualChoicesReviewed.text: Weekly weight for both patients regardless of changing fluid balance

wholeQuestion.question: An adult at high refeeding risk has normal baseline magnesium and phosphate. Under NICE CG32, what is the appropriate laboratory-monitoring approach as support begins?
choices: Obtain baseline values and monitor magnesium and phosphate daily while refeeding risk is present, adapting frequency if instability requires it
Repeat magnesium and phosphate only if symptoms appear because baseline values are normal
Measure glucose regularly but defer magnesium and phosphate until the stable weekly schedule
Measure magnesium and phosphate once weekly from initiation because there is no baseline deficit
wholeQuestion.rationale: NICE Table 2 calls for baseline magnesium and phosphate and daily testing when refeeding risk is present. A normal baseline does not establish that subsequent electrolyte shifts will not occur. The table is chiefly for parenteral nutrition and may be selectively used for at-risk oral or enteral support; more frequent assessment may be needed in acute instability.
